passage: Neelam, you asked why I keep an extra lamp by the door. Listen to your Charu Nani. When I was nine, the power went every evening in our town. Our house had a generator, so I did homework under a bright bulb. One night I walked to the shop with Papa and saw my friend Shabnam sitting under the streetlight by the post office, copying sums and squinting. Next day I asked Amma, "Why does Shabnam study outside?" Amma said their house had no generator. My face went hot. I even said, "It's not my fault!" though nobody had said it was. But after that I kept asking why. Some evenings Shabnam came over, and we shared my bulb.

qa.q: Where was Shabnam studying?
qa.a: Under the streetlight by the post office, copying sums.

qa.q: Why did Charu burst out with "It's not my fault!" when nobody had blamed anyone?
qa.a: Charu felt guilty and a bit defensive on seeing the difference, so the words came out as if pushing blame away.

qa.q: What choice did young Charu make after that hot-faced moment, and what did it change?
qa.a: Charu kept asking why and invited Shabnam over to share the bright bulb, turning an uncomfortable feeling into something useful.

qa.q: What might those evenings under the streetlight have been like for Shabnam?
qa.a: Shabnam was probably used to squinting and just getting the sums done; sharing the bulb may have felt kind, as long as it came as friendship and not pity.

grounding: A child notices that a friend studies under a streetlight while their own home has light, feels guilty and defensive, and starts to ask why.

passage: The rain came down so hard that the headmistress sent everyone home at noon. Kishore climbed into the yellow school van, dry under his raincoat. Through the steamy window he saw Dolma tie a plastic bag over her books and start up the steep path behind the school, alone. "Uncle, why doesn't the van go to Dolma's side?" "No road there, only steps. Forty minutes' walk." Forty minutes. Kishore got home in five. He felt strange, as if he'd taken something without asking. Next morning he asked Dolma, "Do you walk every day? Even in exams?" "Every day," she said, shrugging. "I learn my spellings on the steps." That night Kishore asked his mother why some roads just stop.

qa.q: How long is Dolma's walk home?
qa.a: Forty minutes' walk, up steps.

qa.q: What was Kishore feeling after he got home dry?
qa.a: He felt strange and a little guilty, as if he'd taken something without asking, because his ride was so much easier than Dolma's walk.

qa.q: What did Kishore do with that uneasy feeling, and why was it a good choice?
qa.a: He asked questions, first Dolma and then his mother, instead of looking away, which is how he started to understand that some children begin further back.

qa.q: How might Dolma see the walk, compared with how Kishore sees it?
qa.a: For Dolma it is simply every day, and she even uses it to learn spellings, while to Kishore it suddenly looks long and unfair 🤔

grounding: A child driven home in the rain sees a classmate climb a long path alone and starts asking why their starting points are so different.

passage: So, Chacha, you asked about the state orchestra. I'm Divyansh, first violin, yes, thank you. But the day the list came out, Tamanna, who plays viola, said, "Of course you got in. You've had a private teacher since you were five. I learnt from videos on a borrowed viola." I got so angry. I said, "I practised two hours every single day! Nobody handed me anything!" and walked off. I was fuming the whole way home. That night I sat with the violin case open and thought about it properly. The two hours were real. My blisters were real. But so was the teacher, and the good violin, and Mamma driving me to every lesson. Tamanna practised too, just without any of that. Both things are true, and the second one doesn't erase the first. I haven't said this to Tamanna yet. I'm working out how.

qa.q: How did Tamanna learn to play?
qa.a: From videos, on a borrowed viola.

qa.q: Why did Divyansh get so angry at Tamanna's words?
qa.a: Divyansh felt the two hours of daily practice were being brushed aside, as if the place had simply been handed over, so the comment felt like an attack.

qa.q: What turning point came that night, and where could it lead?
qa.a: Sitting with the violin case, Divyansh saw that the practice and the head start were both real; the next step is telling Tamanna so, without taking back the effort.

qa.q: How might Tamanna have felt when the list went up?
qa.a: Tamanna had practised on a borrowed viola with no teacher, so the list may have felt like proof the race was uneven, whatever effort Divyansh put in.

grounding: A teenager told they had it easier snaps back about daily practice, then sees that the hard work and the head start are both true.

passage: I'm Harpreet, and I was holding the water bottles when it happened. Devika had just won the inter-school tennis final. She was glowing. Nilesh, who'd lost in the semis, shook her hand and said, "Well played. Bit easier with a club court and a coach, though." He said it quietly, not nastily. Devika's face changed. "Excuse me? I'm up at five every day. I've cried on that court. You think it's easy?" She grabbed her bag and walked off. Nilesh just stood there. He practises on the cracked concrete court behind the municipal school, with a racket he taped up himself. On the bus back, Devika was quiet, staring out. Near her stop she said, not to anyone exactly, "The five a.m. is real. The coach is real too, I suppose." I don't know if she'll say it to Nilesh. I hope so.

qa.q: Where does Nilesh practise?
qa.a: On the cracked concrete court behind the municipal school.

qa.q: What does Devika's quiet line on the bus suggest she was beginning to feel and think?
qa.a: It suggests her anger was cooling into an uneasy honesty: her early mornings were real, and so was the advantage of a coach and a club court.

qa.q: What choice does Devika face after the bus ride, and what might she say?
qa.a: She can stay defensive or go back to Nilesh; she might say, "I did work hard, and you're right that I had help you didn't."

qa.q: How might the final have looked to Nilesh, with his taped-up racket?
qa.a: Nilesh wasn't denying her effort, only naming the uneven start, and her anger may have left him feeling he wasn't allowed to say it 😔

grounding: A teenager who wins is told it came easier with a coach, reacts as if attacked, and later begins to see that hard work and advantage can both be true.

subtype: Living with a disadvantage others do not see [Receiver]
passage:
Week one of engineering college. Eshaan learnt that his lab partner Raghav had done two years of entrance coaching, owned a new laptop, and had an uncle who ran a software firm. Eshaan had studied from secondhand books at a government school; he was the first in his family at college.
Mid-semester. Raghav failed a quiz and shrugged. "Dad'll get me a tutor." Eshaan had failed the same quiz. He spent the night in the library, doing every problem twice. Walking back to the hostel at two a.m., he felt it bitterly: they had started at different lines, and nobody even seemed to notice.
End of semester. The results went up. Eshaan had passed every subject, only a little behind Raghav. The old sting came, and then something warmer. He rang home from the hostel corridor. "Amma, I passed everything. All of it." She cried. He grinned at the peeling wall.

qa.q: Where did Eshaan spend the night after failing the quiz?
qa.a: In the library, doing every problem twice.

qa.q: What did Eshaan feel on the walk back at two a.m.?
qa.a: He felt bitter resentment that he and Raghav had started at different lines while nobody else seemed to notice.

qa.q: At the end of the semester, what did Eshaan choose to focus on, and why did it matter?
qa.a: He felt the sting of comparison but chose to ring his mother and share his pride in passing everything, measuring how far he had come rather than only the gap.

qa.q: How might Raghav see the same semester?
qa.a: To Raghav a failed quiz was just a reason to get a tutor, so he may not realise how much harder the same result was for Eshaan.

grounding: A first-generation student sees a peer's coaching, laptop and family safety net, feels the race began at different lines, and also feels proud of how far he has come.

subtype: Living with a disadvantage others do not see [Receiver]
passage: Shreya, you rang me angry that your hostel friends fly home every long weekend while you save for the bus. Let your Vasudha Mami tell you something. In 1994 I was eighteen, at medical college, a tailor's daughter. Half my batch had doctor parents: textbooks at home, uncles who would "have a word" with a professor, fathers who paid if anyone failed. I photocopied chapters page by page. In second year, when a girl got a hospital posting through her father's phone call, I cried in the bathroom, furious. It wasn't fair, and it still isn't. But that same year I stitched my own white coat on Appa's machine, and I topped anatomy. Both things sat in me together, the anger and the pride. Keep both, beta. Don't let either one eat the other.

qa.q: What did Vasudha stitch on Appa's machine?
qa.a: Vasudha's own white coat.

qa.q: Why did Vasudha cry in the bathroom in second year?
qa.a: Vasudha was furious and hurt that a classmate got a posting through a father's phone call, a safety net Vasudha never had.

qa.q: What advice does Vasudha give Shreya, and why might it help?
qa.a: To keep both the anger and the pride without letting either eat the other, so Shreya can name the unfairness and still value the distance covered.

qa.q: How might Shreya hear this story right after an angry phone call?
qa.a: Shreya may feel understood rather than scolded, because the story admits the unfairness is real while showing someone who still went far 🤍

grounding: An elder recalls being a tailor's child among well-connected classmates, resenting their safety nets and feeling proud of the distance covered.

passage: Honestly, Mitra? My father's friend runs the press. I'm Hansa, twenty-four, and I won't pretend my English-medium school and that one phone call didn't help. They did. So when the press asked me to find two more translators for the children's series, I didn't just ring my college friends, who all sound like me. I put up a notice in the district library and sent it to a teachers' group. That's how I found Vasudha, who teaches at a town school and translates better than I do. At our first meeting she said our glossary used city words no village child would know. I wanted to defend it. I wrote her point down instead. We changed forty words. I don't wake up guilty about the head start every morning, and I don't hide it either. I just try to hold the door open the way someone held it for me.

qa.q: Where did Hansa put up the notice for translators?
qa.a: In the district library, and it went to a teachers' group too.

qa.q: When Vasudha criticised the glossary, what did Hansa feel, and what does writing the point down show?
qa.a: Hansa's first urge was to defend the glossary, but writing the point down shows a real wish to listen to someone who sees what Hansa can't.

qa.q: Which choice at the hiring stage made the biggest difference?
qa.a: Instead of ringing college friends who all sound alike, Hansa widened the search, which brought in Vasudha, the better translator.

qa.q: How might Vasudha see this way of working?
qa.a: Vasudha probably felt taken seriously: invited on merit, then heard about the city words, which could make the partnership feel equal.

grounding: A young professional openly owns a head start from family contacts and schooling, shares an opportunity fairly and listens to someone with less, without guilt or denial.

passage: I'm Rafael, and I share a cubicle wall with Siddharth at the law firm. Everyone knows his mother is a judge; he's never hidden it. What I've noticed is what he does with it. Last month the partner said, "Sid, find me a good intern, maybe from your circle." Siddharth came back with three CVs from colleges nobody here had heard of, and his cousin's. The partner picked Nikita, from a small-town law college. Siddharth spent her first week sitting with her through the filing system and never called it a favour. On Friday at lunch Nikita mentioned she'd had to learn legal English from scratch, and he didn't jump in with "me too". He listened, then asked what had helped most. I don't know what he feels about his head start. He doesn't make speeches about it. He just keeps opening the drawer a little wider.

qa.q: Whose CVs did Siddharth bring to the partner?
qa.a: Three from colleges nobody there had heard of, and his cousin's.

qa.q: What does Siddharth's choice not to say "me too" at lunch suggest about him?
qa.a: It suggests he felt respectful of Nikita's experience and wanted to hear it rather than turn it toward himself, though Rafael can't know what he feels about his head start.

qa.q: Which of Siddharth's choices used his advantage most responsibly?
qa.a: Widening the intern search beyond his own circle, then quietly helping Nikita settle without calling it a favour, turned his access into an opening for someone else.

qa.q: What might Nikita's first week have felt like with Siddharth's help?
qa.a: Nikita probably felt welcomed rather than patronised, since the help came quietly and was never framed as charity.

grounding: A colleague watches a young lawyer from a well-connected family share opportunities fairly and listen to someone with less, without speeches or denial.

passage: The drawing competition was in a school hall so noisy with parents and loudspeakers that Gurleen could barely think. Twenty minutes left. Gurleen liked her river, until she glanced at Gopika's paper: a whole village, with tiny goats. Suddenly her river looked thin. She looked again. And again. Each time, Gopika's picture seemed better and hers worse. Ten minutes left, and only half her sky was coloured. Gopika won a certificate; Gurleen got nothing. On the way home she said, "I'm bad at drawing." Papa said, "Last week you told me you were the best in class." Gurleen thought. "That was when I only saw Nimmi's."

qa.q: How much time was left when Gurleen first glanced at Gopika's paper?
qa.a: Twenty minutes.

qa.q: How did Gurleen feel each time she looked at Gopika's drawing?
qa.a: She felt smaller each time; Gopika's picture seemed better and hers worse, though she had liked her river before.

qa.q: What went wrong during the competition, and what could Gurleen try next time?
qa.a: Checking Gopika's paper again and again used up her time, so half the sky stayed blank; next time she could keep her eyes on her own river until the end.

qa.q: How might Papa see Gurleen's two opposite claims about her drawing?
qa.a: Papa can see that her opinion of herself swings with whoever she compares against, so the ranking, not the drawing, is shaping how she feels.

grounding: A child keeps checking a classmate's drawing during a noisy competition and feels smaller each time, showing how constant ranking colours self-worth.

passage: In the Pune housing society's skating class, every child had a sticker chart. Mahima checked everyone's before she even tied her skates. Eshaan: four stickers. Hers: six. She skated faster that evening, grinning. On Thursday a new girl, Sia, arrived with ten stickers from her old class. Mahima's legs felt heavy. She fell twice and told the coach she had a tummy ache. Walking home past the vegetable carts, Eshaan asked, "Why are you sad? You learnt the turn today." Mahima blinked. She had forgotten the turn completely. "I did, na?" She tried it again on the society path, wobbling, and laughed.

qa.q: How many stickers did Sia have?
qa.a: Ten stickers, from her old class.

qa.q: Why did Mahima tell the coach she had a tummy ache?
qa.a: She felt small and deflated after seeing Sia's ten stickers, and wanted a way out of skating while she felt like that.

qa.q: What turning point did Eshaan's question create for Mahima?
qa.a: By reminding her she learnt the turn today, Eshaan helped her notice her own progress instead of the sticker count, and she happily tried it again 🙂

qa.q: How might Eshaan feel about being counted against Mahima's chart?
qa.a: With four stickers, Eshaan might feel ranked below her, yet he still noticed her progress kindly, which suggests he wasn't keeping score the same way.

grounding: A child ranks friends by skating stickers and feels proud or small by turns, until a friend's question points her back to her own progress.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 10, Wednesday.
Anjali has seemed flat all week. During free period I found her in the library corner scrolling, not reading. On her screen: Anirban at a robotics camp, a cousin at a beach, a senior holding a trophy. Without looking up she said, "Everyone is doing something. I'm just... here." I asked what she had done since Sunday. She shrugged. Then, slowly: helped her grandmother with the pension forms, fixed the class projector, finished a whole novel. I said none of those would ever make a photo. She almost smiled. Later I happened to see Anirban's caption under that camp picture: "Day 3, lost every round, so tired." None of that showed in the photo. I have invited Anjali to the Friday reading group, and I will check on her again on Monday.

qa.q: What had Anjali done since Sunday?
qa.a: Helped her grandmother with the pension forms, fixed the class projector, and finished a whole novel.

qa.q: What does Anjali's "I'm just... here" suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: She felt dull and left behind, measuring her ordinary week against everyone else's highlights.

qa.q: Which move by the teacher helped most, and why?
qa.a: Asking what Anjali had actually done since Sunday let her see her own week clearly, without a lecture about social media.

qa.q: How did Anirban's week at the camp really go, judging by the caption?
qa.a: By day 3 Anirban had lost every round and was very tired, so the glossy camp photo hid a hard, ordinary week, much like anyone's.

grounding: A teacher notices a student scrolling peers' polished posts and feeling dull and behind, and helps her see her own ordinary week beside their highlights.

passage:
Saturday, 11:40 pm
Should be asleep. Instead: forty minutes on Kiran's page. Kiran at the state quiz. Kiran's new haircut. Kiran's family at a hill station. Kiran with a certificate for something I didn't even know existed. My Saturday was maths tuition, washing my school shoes, and minding Chhotu so Mummy could nap. I feel like a grey sticker in a colourful album.
Then I remembered: last month I posted ONE photo, the cake I made for Papa's birthday. It looked perfect. Nobody saw the first cake, which sank in the middle and made Chhotu cry. So maybe Kiran's page is the second cake every time.
Still feel grey. Slightly less.
Phone is going in the drawer now.
Pooja

qa.q: What photo did Pooja post last month?
qa.a: The cake made for Papa's birthday.

qa.q: What does "a grey sticker in a colourful album" show about how Pooja feels?
qa.a: Pooja feels small and left out, as if an ordinary Saturday doesn't count next to Kiran's bright highlights.

qa.q: What thought changed the night, and what small choice followed?
qa.a: Remembering the sunken first cake made Pooja realise Kiran's page may show only the best versions too, and the phone went into the drawer.

qa.q: How might Kiran see that same page?
qa.a: Kiran knows the ordinary or failed moments behind each post and may have no idea anyone felt small looking at them.

grounding: A teenager scrolls a peer's highlights late at night, feels dull and behind, then remembers that posts show only the best moments.

passage: The cyclone warning had shut the campus, the hostel generator ran only the corridor lights, and the next internship deadline was midnight tomorrow. By candlelight, Elizabeth read out her acceptance from the marine research station, then apologised for being so happy. Preeti hugged her. Then she lay on her bed in the dark, thinking: of course. Elizabeth is brilliant. I'll never get anything like that. She didn't open her laptop. At ten, Elizabeth sat on the edge of Preeti's bed. "I got rejected by four places first. Want to see my first draft? It was awful." It was. Preeti laughed out loud. Elizabeth's success suddenly looked less like a mountain and more like a staircase. With nineteen percent battery, Preeti opened her own statement and started cutting the first paragraph.

qa.q: How many places rejected Elizabeth first?
qa.a: Four places.

qa.q: What was Preeti thinking as she lay in the dark after the hug?
qa.a: She was sinking into envy and self-doubt, sure that Elizabeth was brilliant and that she herself would never get anything like it.

qa.q: What turned the comparison from crushing to useful?
qa.a: Seeing Elizabeth's four rejections and awful first draft made the goal look reachable, like a staircase, so Preeti opened the laptop and started editing.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth have felt reading out the news beside a friend who was struggling?
qa.a: Elizabeth seemed torn between joy and worry about hurting Preeti, which is why she apologised for being happy and later shared her rejections.

grounding: A student's envy of a friend's internship first stops her working, then turns into motivation once the friend's path looks reachable.

passage: In the college canteen in Dadar, the news went round fast: Rashid had got an articleship at a big audit firm. Gautam and Usha read the message together over cutting chai. Gautam whistled. "He cleared the intermediate one month before us. If he can, we can by March." He started listing firms on a paper napkin. Usha smiled and said nothing. On the local train home she scrolled through Rashid's profile, his neat marks, his confident photo, and felt her stomach drop. Rashid had always been ahead; she had already failed one paper. What was the point? At home she didn't open her books. She re-read the message until the words stopped meaning anything. Next day Gautam waved the napkin at her. "I've marked ten firms. Take five?" Usha looked at the list for a long moment and couldn't answer.

qa.q: What did Gautam write on the paper napkin?
qa.a: A list of firms; he marked ten.

qa.q: Why did Usha feel her stomach drop on the train?
qa.a: She compared herself with Rashid, who had always been ahead, and with one failed paper the goal felt out of reach, so envy slid into self-criticism.

qa.q: When Gautam offers five firms, what small step could help Usha?
qa.a: She could take even one or two firms and make a plan for the failed paper, turning a far-off goal into something she can reach.

qa.q: Why might Gautam and Usha react so differently to the same news?
qa.a: Gautam sees Rashid as just a month ahead, so the goal feels close; Usha, carrying a failed paper, sees the news as proof she is too far behind.

grounding: Two students hear of a friend's articleship; one is spurred on because the goal feels close, while the other sinks into envy because it feels out of reach.

subtype: Feeling small at a friend's success [Receiver]
passage: I'm Anand. Last spring Nilesh and I were both line cooks at the same restaurant, two years in, same burn marks on our wrists. Then the owner made Nilesh sous chef. He pulled me into the cold room to tell me first, eyes shining. I hugged him and meant it. Then I went home and scrubbed an already clean pan for twenty minutes. For a week I was too cheerful, all "Yes, Chef!" jokes, and Nilesh kept giving me odd looks. Finally, over staff dinner, I said it. "I'm really happy for you. And it stings a bit, because I wanted it too. Both are true." Nilesh put down his fork. "Thank God. I thought you were angry with me." We both laughed. Then I said congratulations again, properly this time, and it came out lighter.

qa.q: What job did the owner give Nilesh?
qa.a: Sous chef.

qa.q: What does scrubbing an already clean pan for twenty minutes suggest about Anand's feelings?
qa.a: It suggests Anand was stung and restless underneath the real happiness, with nowhere to put the mixed feelings yet.

qa.q: What choice at staff dinner changed things, and why did it work?
qa.a: Anand admitted being happy and stung at once instead of over-cheering, which cleared the air so the second congratulations could be genuine.

qa.q: How had the week of "Yes, Chef!" jokes looked to Nilesh?
qa.a: Nilesh sensed something was off and feared Anand was angry, so the honest admission came as a relief 😅

grounding: A young adult whose close friend is promoted feels happy and stung together, and admitting both honestly makes real congratulation possible.

subtype: Feeling small at a friend's success [Receiver]
passage:
Coach's note, city athletics club, Saturday.
The selection list arrived this morning: Uma is in the state relay squad. Dolma is not. They have trained side by side for three years. Dolma hugged Uma first, loudly and fast, then went off to run extra laps nobody had set. I let her run. Afterwards she sat on the bench, untying and retying one shoe. I asked how she was. She said, "I'm so happy for her. I'm also jealous, and I hate that." I told her both can sit together, and saying it is better than hiding it. At the end of practice she went over to Uma again, slower this time, and said something I couldn't hear. Uma laughed and cried a little. I have booked a session with Dolma on Tuesday to plan next season.

qa.q: How long have Dolma and Uma trained side by side?
qa.a: Three years.

qa.q: What does Dolma untying and retying one shoe suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she was unsettled, caught between feelings she hadn't sorted out yet: happy for Uma and stung at the same time.

qa.q: What helped Dolma move from a fast hug to a real congratulation?
qa.a: Saying the jealousy out loud and hearing that both feelings can sit together let her return to Uma calmly and congratulate her properly.

qa.q: How might Uma have experienced the two hugs?
qa.a: The first, quick hug may have felt a little hollow; the slower second talk likely felt real, which is why Uma laughed and cried 🤍

grounding: A coach sees an athlete feel both glad and jealous when her training partner is selected, admit it honestly, and then offer a genuine congratulation.

passage: Anirban, you've refreshed that alumni group all morning. Sit with your old Deepak sir a minute. Fifteen years ago, twenty-five and new at this agency, I did the same. Every evening, batchmates' posts: Singapore, a startup, a car. I'd come in next day feeling like a failure. One Sunday I found my notebook from the year before, my first month's to-do lists. "Learn the layout software." "Don't freeze in client meetings." I laughed out loud. I'd done all of it. So I made a rule: once a month, I compared myself only with that notebook. I muted the six people whose posts always flattened me; didn't unfriend anyone, just stopped looking. And I picked two people, Farzana and old Mr Pillai, whose work I truly wanted to learn from, and asked them to lunch. That's the whole trick. Now, what's in your notebook from last year?

qa.q: How many people did Deepak mute?
qa.a: Six people, the ones whose posts always flattened Deepak.

qa.q: Why did Deepak laugh out loud at the old notebook?
qa.a: Deepak suddenly saw real progress: every worry from the year before, like the layout software and client meetings, had been handled.

qa.q: Which of Deepak's choices kept the useful side of comparison?
qa.a: Picking Farzana and Mr Pillai to learn from kept comparison as a teacher, while muting the six removed the part that only hurt.

qa.q: How might Anirban take the closing question about last year's notebook?
qa.a: Anirban may feel gently steered from the alumni group toward personal progress, without being told how to feel.

grounding: A senior colleague recalls measuring progress against the previous year, muting accounts that flattened the mood, and choosing a few peers to learn from.

passage: Rustam's self-appraisal was due at nine, the office Wi-Fi kept dropping, and the only free charger was across the room. Worse, the team chat kept pinging with Deepika's news: a conference talk, a client award. Rustam's own draft felt thin. The old habit whispered: compare. Instead, Rustam opened last year's appraisal. "Needs close supervision on client calls." This year Rustam had run eleven calls alone. That line went in first. Then Rustam muted the loud industry group that always left a sour taste and typed to Deepika: "Congrats on the talk! Could you show me how you structured it, sometime next week?" A thumbs-up came back 👍. At 8:52, the Wi-Fi held long enough to submit.

qa.q: How many client calls had Rustam run alone this year?
qa.a: Eleven calls.

qa.q: What did Rustam feel as Deepika's news kept pinging?
qa.a: Rustam felt insecure about the thin draft and was tugged by the old habit of measuring up against Deepika's achievements.

qa.q: What turning point shaped the appraisal, and why was it a good choice?
qa.a: Opening last year's appraisal let Rustam measure against "needs close supervision" and lead with real growth, instead of against someone else's highlights.

qa.q: How might Deepika read Rustam's message?
qa.a: Deepika would likely feel appreciated rather than envied, since the message congratulates first and then asks to learn.

grounding: A young professional under deadline measures progress against last year, mutes a group that drags the mood down, and chooses to learn from one peer.

passage:
"Jomon, sums done?"
"No, Ammachi. I'm slow, na. Kishore chettan does them fast."
"Try the first one."
"Why? Everyone says I'm slow. Even Miss."
"Kishore, help your brother."
"Ammachi, I'm doing the Olympiad paper. The hard one. Miss says I'm her clever boy."
"See? He gets the hard ones," Jomon said, and put his pencil down. "I get the easy ones and I still get them wrong."
"Who untangled the whole kite string yesterday? Two hours, all by himself?"
"...Me."
"Slow boys can't do that."
Jomon looked at the first sum for a long time. Then he picked up the pencil again.

qa.q: What was Kishore working on instead of helping?
qa.a: The Olympiad paper, the hard one.

qa.q: Why did Jomon put his pencil down?
qa.a: He believed the 'slow' label everyone used, so trying felt pointless next to his clever brother.

qa.q: What did Ammachi do that helped Jomon pick the pencil up again?
qa.a: She reminded him that he untangled the kite string for two hours by himself, giving him real evidence against the 'slow' label.

qa.q: How has the 'clever boy' label shaped Kishore differently?
qa.a: Being called clever makes Kishore reach for the hard Olympiad paper, while Jomon, called slow, gives up; the labels are steering both boys.

grounding: A boy repeatedly called slow stops trying while his brother, called clever, takes on hard work, until a grandmother points to evidence against the label.

passage: Last year, in Class 5, the dance teacher always called me "Lazy Kavitha", because I came late once. After that, whenever the steps got hard, I thought, why try, I'm the lazy one anyway. I stood at the back and moved slowly. Then, in the new term, Mehak Miss came. On the first day she said, "Kavitha, you have good balance. Can you try the spin at the front?" Nobody had said I had anything good. I practised the spin in our corridor every night. I fell a lot. At the annual day, I did it in the front row. I still think about how one word made me slow, and another made me try.

qa.q: What did the dance teacher call Kavitha?
qa.a: "Lazy Kavitha".

qa.q: How did Kavitha feel whenever the steps got hard?
qa.a: Kavitha felt discouraged and thought, 'why try, I'm the lazy one anyway', because the label had become part of how Kavitha saw things.

qa.q: What choice did Kavitha make after Mehak Miss's words, and what came of it?
qa.a: Kavitha practised the spin in the corridor every night, falling a lot, and finally did it in the front row at the annual day.

qa.q: How might Mehak Miss have seen Kavitha on that first day?
qa.a: Mehak Miss saw good balance, not a lazy child, perhaps because the old label had never reached the new teacher.

grounding: A child labelled lazy starts trying less, and a new teacher's belief leads the child to take on a hard spin.
